summary: This RFC defines a Telnet option for passing a 64-bit terminal location number, from a system created at CMU to find where a user is logged in from. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 946 proposes a Telnet option for sending a terminal location number to a remote host. The number combines a host address with a terminal number so system software can identify where a user connected from.

questions: what is the telnet terminal location number option
how does telnet report a user's location
what is the telnet ttyloc option
what is the terminal location number
subtitle: A Telnet option for sending a compact terminal and host location identifier.

tldr.problem: A remote host may know the connecting host's name but lack information about which terminal or location the user is connecting from.
tldr.mechanism: The Telnet peers negotiate TTYLOC, then the client sends a 64-bit value containing a host address and a terminal number.
tldr.outcome: The option carries a compact identifier that server software can pass to operating-system or other system components.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 946's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC presents the TTYLOC Telnet option as a proposal and requests discussion.

sections.title: Why Pass a Terminal Location Number
sections.content:
The RFC describes systems that can use login-location information to help identify where a user is located or how to contact them. For incoming network connections, a host may otherwise know only the remote host name.

TTYLOC was designed as a compact value that can pass through operating-system and network layers with few software changes. The memo presents it as a shorthand for hosts in a shared community, not as a replacement for the existing Telnet Terminal Location option.
sections.plainLanguage: A host name alone may not tell a system which terminal a user is using. TTYLOC adds a compact terminal identifier to the Telnet connection.

sections.title: The 64-Bit TTYLOC Value
sections.content:
TTYLOC consists of two 32-bit numbers: an ARPA Internet host address and a number for a terminal on that host. The address 0.0.0.0 means unknown; terminal value FFFFFFFF means unknown, and FFFFFFFE means detached.

The bytes are sent from most significant to least significant. The option's subnegotiation identifies format 0 before the 64-bit value.
sections.plainLanguage: The value contains a host address followed by a terminal number. Special values can say that the host or terminal is unknown or that the process has no terminal.

sections.title: Negotiating and Sending TTYLOC
sections.content:
The user-side Telnet can offer to send TTYLOC with WILL TTYLOC, and the server can accept with DO TTYLOC. After agreement, the client sends the number in a subnegotiation.

The server may initiate by requesting TTYLOC, after which the user side can agree and send the value. The RFC recommends trying the existing SEND-LOCATION option if sending TTYLOC is refused.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server first agree to use TTYLOC. The client then sends the host and terminal number to the server.
